GUIDES.title: Abu Simbel from Aswan: How to Plan the Day
GUIDES.excerpt: How to plan a visit to Abu Simbel from Aswan: what you will see in the two temples of Ramesses II, how they were saved from Lake Nasser, road, air or a Lake Nasser cruise, private or shared tours, and the February and October sun days.
blocks: Abu Simbel is the one day of an Egypt trip that most people plan around. The two rock temples of Ramesses II stand far to the south of Aswan, near the Sudanese border, so the visit takes a full day away from the city. This guide covers what you will see, how the temples were saved, the ways to get there, and how to choose between the tours on offer.

Carved out of a sandstone cliff on the west bank of the Nile, the Great Temple is fronted by four seated statues of Ramesses II, each about 20 metres high, two on either side of the entrance. Small figures of his queen Nefertari, his mother and his children stand around their feet. Inside, three halls run some 56 metres into the rock, lined with statues of the king in the form of Osiris and with scenes of his campaign at the Battle of Kadesh. The temple is dedicated to the sun gods Amun-Ra and Ra-Horakhty.
Just to the north stands a smaller temple, dedicated to Queen Nefertari for the worship of the goddess Hathor. Its façade carries standing statues of the king and the queen, about 10.5 metres high.
On the southern colossi, look for graffiti left by Greek mercenaries serving Egypt in the 6th century BC. They are among the early evidence for the Greek alphabet.

When the Aswan High Dam was built, the rising waters of Lake Nasser threatened to submerge Abu Simbel. Between 1963 and 1968, an international team, funded by more than 50 countries, cut away the top of the cliff, took both temples apart and rebuilt them on higher ground, about 60 metres above their original site. It was part of the UNESCO campaign of 1960 to 1980 that moved the temples of Nubia, and Abu Simbel is now part of the World Heritage site Nubian Monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae, inscribed in 1979.
By road from Aswan. The usual choice. Tours leave Aswan before dawn and return in the afternoon, so most of the day is spent in the vehicle. Most include hotel pickup.
By air. Short flights from Aswan save the long drive, at a higher cost. Check the flight times against the temple visit you want.
By Lake Nasser cruise. Cruises on Lake Nasser between Aswan and Abu Simbel reach the temples by water. Other temples moved during the rescue, such as Wadi es-Sebua and Amada, stand by the lake.
Day trips from Aswan come in two main forms:
Private tours. A car and driver for you alone, often with an Egyptologist guide. You agree the pickup time and the pace with the driver.
Shared tours. You join a group in a minibus or coach. They are cheaper and the route is the same, but pickups and timings are fixed.
What to check before you book

• Whether the temple entry tickets are included or paid on the day.
  • Whether a guide comes into the temples or only drives.
  • The pickup time and place, and how long you will have at the site.
  • The cancellation terms, especially around the sun days.
Our Abu Simbel day trip page compares the options we recommend.
The sun days in February and October

On two days of the year, about 22 February and 22 October, the first rays of the morning sun run the full length of the Great Temple and light the statues in the innermost sanctuary. It still happens today, on the rebuilt temple. These mornings bring large crowds and special events, so book well ahead and expect a very early start. On other days you will have more space inside the temples.
Take water, a snack and sun protection. The forecourt has little shade.
Carry a layer for the pre-dawn drive. Desert mornings can be cool in winter.
Photography rules inside the temples can change. Follow the guards.
Leave the rest of the day free. Plan Philae, a felucca and the Nubian villages in Aswan for the days before or after.
toc: The sun days in February and October
faq: How far is Abu Simbel from Aswan?
Far to the south, near the border with Sudan. Most visitors go on a day trip by road or take a short flight.
Is a private tour worth it?
If you want a guide inside the temples and a flexible pace, yes. A shared tour sees the same temples for less, with fixed timings.
When does the sun reach the sanctuary?
On or around 22 February and 22 October, at sunrise. On those days the temples are at their busiest.
Can I see both temples on a day trip?
Yes. The Great Temple and the Small Temple stand next to each other, and day trips include both.

GUIDES.title: The Best Time to Visit Egypt, Month by Month
GUIDES.excerpt: When to visit Egypt, season by season and region by region: the Nile Valley's comfortable winter, the Red Sea's long beach season, the desert's cold nights, and how Ramadan and holidays change a trip.
blocks: There is no single best month for Egypt, because the country covers very different climates. The Nile Valley has hot deserts on both sides. The Red Sea coasts have long, warm seasons. The Mediterranean coast is milder and wetter, and the Western Desert is extreme in both directions. The right time depends on what you plan to do. This guide goes region by region, then through the calendar.
For temples and sightseeing (Cairo, Luxor, Aswan): October to April, when days are warm rather than scorching.
For the Red Sea (Hurghada, Sharm El Sheikh): most of the year. Spring and autumn give warm water without the summer heat.
For the desert (Siwa, the White Desert): October to April, but pack for cold nights.
For Alexandria and the north coast: spring and autumn. Summer is Egypt's own beach season.
Mild in winter, hot in summer. Sightseeing at Giza is the main thing affected by the heat, because the plateau is exposed. In the warm months, plan it for the early morning.

The heat increases the further south you go. From late spring to early autumn, Luxor and Aswan are among the hottest places in Egypt. Winter is the peak season, with the most comfortable conditions and the most visitors.
Warm for most of the year. Winter is milder on land, with cooler water and more wind (good news for kitesurfers). Late summer and autumn bring the warmest sea.
The most temperate climate in the country, with the sea's humidity. Winter brings some rain and wind. Summer is busy with Egyptian holidaymakers.
Hot by day for much of the year and very hot in summer. In winter, nights in the desert are cold, sometimes near freezing. Pack accordingly.

December to February. Peak season in the Nile Valley: pleasant days, cool evenings and chilly early mornings. Busiest around Christmas and New Year. The Abu Simbel sun festival falls on or around 22 February.
March and April. Warming up, and still excellent for sightseeing. Spring winds can occasionally bring sand.
May to September. Hot to very hot in the south. It's the low season for Nile Valley sightseeing, so plan early starts and midday rests. The Red Sea is in full summer season.
October and November. Temperatures fall and the season restarts. It's an excellent time everywhere. The second Abu Simbel sun festival falls on or around 22 October.

Ramadan follows the Islamic lunar calendar and moves earlier each year. During the month: - opening hours of sites and shops often change; - many people fast from dawn to sunset; - evenings become especially lively and festive.
Travelling during Ramadan is entirely possible and can be memorable. Be discreet about eating and drinking in public during the day, and check opening times.
The Eid holidays after Ramadan and after the Hajj are busy domestic travel periods, particularly on the coasts.
If temples are your priority, travel between October and April, and book early for the Christmas and New Year peak.
If you can only travel in summer, combine early-morning sightseeing with the Red Sea.
If you want the desert, pick spring or autumn for the mildest days and nights.
Ready to plan? See our destination guides for Cairo, Luxor, Aswan and the Red Sea at Hurghada.
faq: What is the worst time to visit Egypt?
For Nile Valley sightseeing, the height of summer, when the south is extremely hot. It's still possible with early starts, and it's the quietest season at the sites.
Is it cold in Egypt in winter?
Days are usually mild to warm, but mornings, evenings and desert nights can be cold. Bring layers.
Is it a good idea to travel during Ramadan?
Yes, with some planning: opening hours change, but the evenings are festive and welcoming.

GUIDES.title: 7 Days in Egypt: The Perfect First Itinerary
GUIDES.excerpt: A realistic first-time Egypt itinerary for seven days: Cairo and the pyramids, Luxor's temples and tombs, and Aswan, with options for a Nile cruise, the Red Sea or Abu Simbel, and what to leave out.
blocks: Seven days is enough for a first taste of Egypt if you accept one rule: stick to the Nile Valley. Cairo, Luxor and Aswan hold most of the monuments people come to see, and they're connected by short flights, trains and the river. Adding the Red Sea, Alexandria or the desert to one week means spending more time in transit than at the sites.
Days 1–3: Cairo. The pyramids, the Grand Egyptian Museum, Islamic and Coptic Cairo.
Days 4–5: Luxor. The East Bank temples and the West Bank tombs.
Days 6–7: Aswan. Philae, the Nile by felucca, and Abu Simbel.
Fly from Cairo to Luxor (or take the overnight train), travel between Luxor and Aswan by road, train or boat, and fly back from Aswan.

+ Day 1 — Arrive in Cairo Arrive, settle in and have an easy first evening. If you have the energy, walk Downtown or eat at a street-food spot. + Day 2 — Giza An early start at the pyramids and the Sphinx, then the Grand Egyptian Museum in the afternoon. + Day 3 — Old Cairo Coptic Cairo and the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in the morning. Late afternoon on Al-Muizz Street and in Khan el-Khalili. Overnight train, or a morning flight next day, to Luxor. + Day 4 — Luxor, East Bank Karnak in the morning, rest at midday, then Luxor Temple at dusk. + Day 5 — Luxor, West Bank Valley of the Kings, Hatshepsut's temple and Medinet Habu. Optional balloon flight at dawn. + Day 6 — To Aswan Travel south, stopping at Edfu and Kom Ombo if you go by road. Philae temple, and a felucca at sunset. + Day 7 — Abu Simbel, then home A pre-dawn trip to Abu Simbel (or a morning on Elephantine Island if you'd rather rest), then fly to Cairo for your connection.
Transfers take longer than they look on a map. Leave a buffer on your departure day, and avoid booking a very early international flight on the day you return from Aswan.

Replace days 4–7 with a 3- or 4-night Luxor–Aswan cruise. It visits Edfu and Kom Ombo on the way, and your hotel moves with you. Give Luxor an extra day before or after, because cruise stops are short.
Drop Aswan and go from Luxor to Hurghada by road for two or three days of reefs. You'll lose Abu Simbel and Philae.
If seven days feels rushed, drop Abu Simbel and give each city an extra half-day. Most people who return to Egypt say they wish they'd slowed down the first time.
What to leave for next time
Alexandria, Siwa and the Western Desert, Sinai and a longer Red Sea stay each deserve their own trip. Trying to squeeze them into one week means you see none of them properly.

Luxor guide: the two banks, tombs and balloons.
Aswan guide: Philae, Nubia and Abu Simbel.
toc: What to leave for next time
faq: Is seven days enough for Egypt?
Enough for the highlights of the Nile Valley, with early starts. Ten days lets you add a cruise or the Red Sea at a gentler pace.
Should I fly or take the train between Cairo and Luxor?
Flights are faster. The overnight sleeper train saves a hotel night and is an experience in itself. Both work.
Is a Nile cruise better than hotels?
A cruise is relaxing and includes Edfu and Kom Ombo. Hotels give you more time in Luxor and Aswan themselves. It depends on your pace.

GUIDES.title: Cairo Travel Guide: Beyond the Pyramids
GUIDES.excerpt: Cairo beyond the pyramids: a neighbourhood-by-neighbourhood guide to Islamic Cairo, Coptic Cairo, Downtown, Zamalek and the Nile, with a walking route through the old city and tips for everyday Cairo.
blocks: Most visitors see Cairo through the pyramids and the new museum at Giza, then leave. This guide is about the rest of the city: the neighbourhoods where Cairenes live, pray, shop and eat. It's where Cairo stops being a transit stop and starts being one of the great cities of the world. For the essentials (the sights, where to stay, how many days), start with our Cairo destination guide.
A walk through the old city
This route follows the spine of Fatimid Cairo from north to south. It's best in the late afternoon, when the light softens and the streets fill up:
Start at Bab al-Futuh, one of the northern gates of the medieval city.
Walk south along Al-Muizz Street, past mosques, madrasas and sabil-kuttabs (fountain-schools), some of them restored.
Stop at the Qalawun complex, one of the great Mamluk monuments.
Cross into the lanes of Khan el-Khalili, and take tea at an old café.
Cross the main road to Al-Azhar Mosque.
Continue south through the textile and spice streets to Bab Zuweila, and climb its minarets if they're open.
End with sunset at Al-Azhar Park on the hill above the old city.
Wear shoes with grip, since the streets are uneven. Dress modestly. Keep small notes for tea, entry to monuments and tips. Mosques ask visitors to remove their shoes, and women to cover their hair.
A walled, quiet quarter of churches, the Coptic Museum and the Ben Ezra Synagogue, inside the old Roman fortress of Babylon. Mar Girgis metro station is right beside it.
The 19th-century centre, laid out in a European style, with grand façades, old cinemas, bookshops, galleries and local cafés. Walk it at night, when it's busiest.
The island neighbourhood of Gezira, leafy and cosmopolitan, full of galleries, restaurants and embassies. The Cairo Tower offers a view over the whole city.
Curving streets of old villas and embassies along the Nile, just south of Downtown.
The hilltop fortress, the great mosques of Sultan Hassan and Al-Rifa'i below it, and, a short walk away, the Ibn Tulun mosque and the Gayer-Anderson Museum.
The ahwa. The traditional coffee house is the city's living room: tea, coffee, shisha, backgammon and dominoes. Sitting in one is a rite of passage.
Eating late. Dinner is often late, and many places stay busy past midnight.
Friday. The weekly day of rest. Mornings are quiet, and mosques are busy around the midday prayer.
Traffic. Plan your days by area. Crossing the city at rush hour can take a long time.
End a day with a felucca at sunset from the Corniche, or a dinner cruise with music and a show. For a street-food evening with a local guide, see our night food tour.
toc: A walk through the old city
faq: Is Islamic Cairo safe to walk around?
It's a busy, lived-in area, and walking in daytime and early evening is the normal way to explore it. Use ordinary city precautions with bags and phones, and dress modestly.
How long does the old-city walk take?
Allow a half-day at a relaxed pace, with stops for monuments and tea.
What's the best area for an evening out?
Downtown and Zamalek for cafés and restaurants, and the old city around Khan el-Khalili and Al-Muizz Street for atmosphere.

GUIDES.title: 10 Hidden Gems Most Visitors Never See
GUIDES.excerpt: Ten remarkable places in Egypt that most visitors skip: from the Bent Pyramid and Medinet Habu to Abydos, Dendera, Wadi Al-Hitan and Rosetta, with what makes each special and how to fit it into a trip.
blocks: Most first trips to Egypt follow the same route: Giza, Luxor, Aswan, maybe the Red Sea. That route is popular for good reason. But some of the country's most memorable places sit just off it, and they are often far quieter. These ten are all well-established sites, not secret spots. They're simply the ones that visitors in a hurry tend to leave out.
1. Dahshur: the Bent and Red Pyramids

South of Saqqara, two of the pharaoh Sneferu's pyramids stand in open desert. The Bent Pyramid changes angle halfway up, and you can go inside the Red Pyramid. They belong to the same UNESCO site as Giza, but they usually see a fraction of the visitors.

In the Fayoum desert, fossilised skeletons of early whales lie in the sand, with legs from the era when whales were evolving from land animals. It's Egypt's natural World Heritage site, and a surreal desert landscape. It needs a 4×4 and a long day from Cairo.
3. The Gayer-Anderson Museum and Ibn Tulun
In the middle of Islamic Cairo, a restored Ottoman-era house full of eclectic collections sits beside one of the city's oldest and most serene mosques.
4. Abydos: the Temple of Seti I
One of the most important religious sites of ancient Egypt, with some of the finest reliefs anywhere, and the famous list of kings. It's usually visited as a day trip from Luxor.
A superbly preserved late temple, with painted ceilings and rooftop chapels. It's often combined with Abydos on the same day.
On Luxor's West Bank, the mortuary temple of Ramesses III has deeply carved, still-coloured reliefs. It's usually quieter than the Valley of the Kings.
The village of the craftsmen who built the royal tombs, with their own small, brightly painted tombs. It's an intimate look at everyday life in ancient Thebes.
8. The Monastery of St Simeon, Aswan
The ruins of a fortified desert monastery on Aswan's west bank, reached by boat and a walk or camel ride through the sand.
Where the Rosetta Stone was found, on the Nile's western mouth near Alexandria. Its Ottoman-era merchant houses are the attraction today.
Remote, Amazigh, surrounded by salt lakes and dunes. See our full Siwa guide.

• From Cairo: Dahshur (half-day, easy to add to Saqqara); Wadi Al-Hitan (a long full day).
  • From Luxor: Abydos and Dendera (a full day together); Medinet Habu and Deir el-Medina (add to a West Bank day).
  • From Alexandria: Rosetta (a half or full day).
